absent: Locking, ordering and concurrency rules for register access, clock resume, quirk probing and reboot globals.
Full reboot shutdown and reset sequences beyond DMI-driven method selection.
Complete DMI table contents beyond the shown first part and final registration behavior.
Detailed PCI device table bindings that trigger each quirk and resume handling after suspend.
Exact architectural register, floating-state and debug-register layouts beyond slot counts and access extents shown.

findings.text: Compat ptrace entry selects handling by execution personality and build configuration, preferring an extended 32-bit path when not in legacy 32-bit call context and otherwise using legacy emulation handling, with neutral success when emulation is unavailable.

Extended 32-bit user-area peek and poke accept only naturally aligned offsets inside the user area at or above the segment register region, reject other offsets with an I/O error, expose only the low half of register and debug slots on read, and accept word updates that affect the low portion on write.

Extended whole-register and floating-state requests are satisfied through a shared 64-bit register view using its general and floating slots over full structure extents, while unrecognized requests fall through to a generic compat handler with widened address and data.

The 64-bit register view presents general, floating, extended state, I/O permission and optional shadow-stack slots, each bound to a core-dump note identity and sized by natural word or fixed 64-bit granularity, with counts derived from architectural state sizes and with activity, fetch and store hooks where meaningful.

The 32-bit register view presents general, legacy floating, extended floating, extended state, thread-local storage and I/O permission slots using narrow granularity except for wide extended state, with thread-local entries carrying a segment-table bias and count and the view identifying as legacy Intel; narrow general aliases reuse the common register type and accessors.

Register-view selection for a task inspects current register context for 64-bit mode where emulation is possible and returns the legacy 32-bit view for non-64-bit tasks and the 64-bit view otherwise, with build options determining which branch exists.

Debug trap reporting records a debug fault number and supplied error code in current thread state and forces a trap signal whose fault address is the instruction pointer for user-mode contexts and null otherwise; single-step reporting is a special case using a breakpoint code and zero error.
A globally visible array of 64-bit words reserves space for software-defined extended-state bytes shared with floating-state handling.

Paravirtual clock keeps a rarely written flag byte and a CPU-zero time-info pointer plus a 64-bit monotonic guard initialized to zero; resume reinitializes the guard to zero so later updates are accepted anew.

Chipset interrupt-distribution quirk applies only to early revisions, briefly enables hidden configuration access, samples a fabric control bit on a peer function, and when that bit is clear disables kernel interrupt debugging and affinity handling before restoring the original configuration value.

Forced timer discovery state consists of a global address override initially unset, a resume-action selector distinguishing no action from several vendor families, a cached device pointer for later resume, and a mapped control region pointer used during probing.

Each vendor timer enable routine first gives up if firmware already supplied an address or a previous force succeeded, then either derives an address from existing enable bits or attempts to enable hardware and re-reads to confirm; on success it records the derived address and vendor resume action and caches the device where needed, otherwise it reports failure and releases any mapping. Some families require an explicit user request, one checks revision first, and one claims a fixed high address without resume action.
One quirk unconditionally marks message-signaled timer interrupts as disabled regardless of device identity.

AMD host-bridge quirk locates function zero on the same slot, combines bus-derived node identity with low bits from a configuration word, and assigns the resulting node to the device only when that node is online.
AMD scrub quirk clears a small group of low-order control bits in each of two memory-controller configuration words when any are set, leaving other bits unchanged.
Intel reliability quirks sample capability registers and enable fragile machine-check copy handling when bits indicate an advanced reliability SKU or relevant nonvolatile-memory modes.
A global flag records whether the platform vendor matches Apple, evaluated once during early initialization from system-management identity strings.
Reboot and power control exposes a power-off hook pointer, an emergency indicator, a safety flag for a port-based reset mechanism, and a module-prefixed logging format.

Reboot-method selection is driven by a table matching board or system vendor and product strings to callbacks that set a global reboot type to BIOS, ACPI, EFI, PCI-forced or keyboard paths, skipping redundant updates, guarding EFI selection on runtime availability, and logging the chosen method.
Forced timer addresses are built around a high reserved base in the FED00000 hex region, with low placement bits taken from hardware capability fields or fixed to zero depending on vendor.

User-area ptrace addressing treats the general register block as the low region starting at the segment area for extended access, followed by eight debug registers addressable as consecutive word slots.

Chipset workarounds perform temporary PCI configuration writes, control-region mappings and indexed port accesses; incorrect ordering, missing restoration, or failure to release mappings could leave hidden functions exposed, stale address overrides, or altered interrupt and timer behavior.
